title: Dych chi'n byw yn y tŵr?

provenance.author: block B1 writer (Claude Opus 5.5, model-written)
notes: Beat realised in four sections: the walk to the river (Dafi, riding in Arth's hair, can fly only a short hop), the polite questions on the bank, fishing from the old boat (a yellow fish; Dafi steams the pool and the fish flee), and Pero's swim, which soaks everyone except Myrddin. Ends on Myrddin's 'Dych chi eisiau gweld y byd dan y dŵr?' with Arth 'Ydyn!' and Mali 'Nac ydyn!'.

Primary target G09: about 35 plural / polite forms (dyn ni, dych chi, maen nhw; dyn ni ddim, dych chi ddim, dyn nhw ddim; Ydych / Nac ydych, Ydyn / Nac ydyn; dewch, ewch, edrychwch, arhoswch). Contrasts: Arth's 'wyt ti'n byw yn y tŵr?' corrected by Mali to 'dych chi'; 'Wyt ti'n hoffi'r afon, Dafi?' ↔ 'A chi, Myrddin? Dych chi'n hoffi'r afon?'; Mali's 'Edrych, Arth!' ↔ Arth's 'Edrychwch!'. Only the four productive -wch forms are used.
First use of chi to Myrddin is motivated in the story: Mali, who is exact, corrects Arth ('Mae Myrddin yn hen, ac mae e'n athro. Dim ti: chi!'). Cai also uses chi to Myrddin from here.

Running words about 980 against 900 (window 810–990): besides the episode, the chapter carries next-five-chapter recall for Penodau 4–8 (chwilio, clywed, sŵn, cau ar gau; hud, dysgu, sut, dewin; mainc, gwag, menyn, caws, wy, gofyn, sefyll, bwced, dail, distaw, prysur, coes, clust; marchogaeth, tarian, aur, arian, ffrind, cryf, gwan, trwm, anrheg, pen-blwydd, pymtheg oed). Each sits inside an event (Cai riding to the river, the bench, the empty bucket, Pero shaking himself dry, Cai claiming a birthday fish).

Applied gpt-6-astra review (2026-10-12): Pensum C c3 answer key corrected (Dafi can fly, but not far); B b2 now cues swimming; C c1/c5/c6 accept further correct answers; glosses that were associations rather than synonyms rewritten as define glosses (byw, pysgota, pawb); Gramadeg and the Ydych gloss now show both answer persons (Ydych / Ydyn; Ydw / Ydyn); cy-llyn sense now 'lake; pool'. Not taken: 'mae e'n nofio'n gyflym' for 'mae'r coesau'n gyflym yn y dŵr' (grammatical, and it carries coes recall for Pennod 7).

Continuity with Pennod 11 (written in parallel): Myrddin comes to the river without his hat (it stays by the kitchen fire); Dafi rides in Arth's hair and can fly short hops, so that at the end of Pennod 10 he can fly home alone ahead of the others.
Planted for Pennod 10: 'pysgodyn mawr iawn yn y llyn' under the bridge (the pike); the small yellow fish.

Audit-fix pass 2026-10-19 (docs/reviews/welsh-russian-lessons-2026-10-19.md): the s034–s048 question volley gave Myrddin three river deflections in a row; the middle exchange (s042 'Ond ble dych chi'n byw?' / s043 'Ble mae'r afon yn byw, Mali?') is cut, keeping 'yn y byd…', the age answer (quoted in the Gramadeg) and 'Ydy'r afon yn afon go iawn?' (the continuity log for Pennod 9 still quotes s043 as an example of his sideways answers). Cai's s090 recall inventory ('pysgod a bara, caws a mêl, menyn ac wy!') is now 'Dw i'n hoffi pysgod i frecwast!' (food words recur in Penodau 8 and 11). Glosses that came after first use moved: byw from s038 to s034 (Arth's first question); the pysgodyn · pysgod number gloss and vignette from s068 to s052, Dafi's 'Pysgod!', so s056 and the pysgota gloss at s058 ('eisiau dal pysgod') follow a known word. Pensa: C c3 now accepts 'Ydy, mae Dafi'n gallu hedfan' and similar full answers; A a5 was trivial (the answer was the prompt), now 'Dych chi'n gallu nofio? (Pero)' → 'Wyt ti'n gallu nofio?'; b7 also fitted llyn, now excluded by 'dyn nhw ddim yn y dŵr'; c1/c5/c6 accept 'wrth y bont', pronoun subjects and fuller answers. The review question on s043 is dropped with the segment (it asked: [?] 'Ble mae'r afon yn byw?' (Where does the river live?) as Myrddin's playful counter-question: understandable and natural?). Running words 987 → 967, sentences 140 → 138.

grammar.nodyn_en:
This chapter completes the present tense of bod ('to be') with the plural persons. Person means who a sentence is about (the speaker, the one spoken to, or someone else); plural means more than one. Beside the singular forms dw i ('I am'), rwyt ti ('you are') and mae e / mae hi ('he / she is'), stand dyn ni ('we are'), dych chi ('you are', to more than one person, or politely to one) and maen nhw ('they are'). As before, yn (shortened to 'n after a vowel) links them to a verb-noun, the dictionary form of a verb: Dyn ni'n mynd i'r afon heddiw ('We're going to the river today'), Maen nhw'n byw yno ('They live there'). Before a description, yn softens the next word as usual (except ll and rh): dyn ni'n wlyb ('we're wet', from gwlyb).

Nhw ('they') can mean people (Arth and Mali in the boat) or things (the fish in Maen nhw'n byw yno). Maen goes only with nhw. When the subject is a noun, even a plural noun or two names, the verb stays mae: Mae'r plant yn eistedd wrth Myrddin ('The children sit by Myrddin'). Pawb ('everyone') also takes mae: Mae pawb yn wlyb ('Everyone is wet').

The negative ('not') follows dw i ddim and dyw e ddim: dyn ni ddim ('we are not'), dych chi ddim ('you are not'), and for 'they' dyn nhw ddim, not maen nhw ddim, just as mae e becomes dyw e ddim. Yn still comes before a verb-noun: Dyn ni ddim yn gweld pysgod ('We don't see any fish'), Dych chi ddim yn nofio ('You don't swim'), Dyn nhw ddim yn gwybod ('They don't know'). A place word such as yma ('here') needs no linking yn, as after mae: Dyn nhw ddim yma! ('They aren't here!').

In the southern speech of this book, a question with ni or chi is the statement said as a question: Dych chi'n byw yn y tŵr? ('Do you live in the tower?'), Dyn ni'n pysgota yn y cwch? ('Are we fishing in the boat?'). A question word goes in front: Sut dych chi'n sych? ('How are you dry?'). For a yes/no question about 'them' the story uses Ydyn nhw …?: Ydyn nhw'n fawr? ('Are they big?').

As in Penodau 4 and 5, the answer repeats the verb in the right person: Ydyn and Nac ydyn ('yes', 'no') for 'we' or 'they', Ydych and Nac ydych for 'you'. Choose by who the answer is about. Arth, in the boat, asks Dyn ni'n pysgota yn y cwch?, and Myrddin, on the bank, answers Ydych ('Yes, you are'). Asked Ydyn nhw'n fawr?, he says Ydyn ('Yes, they are'). To Dych chi eisiau gweld y byd dan y dŵr? ('Do you want to see the world under the water?'), Arth answers Ydyn! ('Yes, we do!') and Mali Nac ydyn! ('No, we don't!'). Asked of one person, dych chi gets a singular answer: Dych chi'n hen iawn? ('Are you very old?') Ydw ('Yes, I am').

Chi is also the polite 'you' to one person. Arth asks Myrddin wyt ti'n byw yn y tŵr? ('do you live in the tower?'), and Mali corrects him: Mae Myrddin yn hen, ac mae e'n athro. Dim ti: chi! ('Myrddin is old, and he's a teacher. Not ti: chi!'). The children say chi to Myrddin but ti to Dafi and Pero: Wyt ti'n hoffi'r afon, Dafi? ('Do you like the river, Dafi?') beside A chi, Myrddin? Dych chi'n hoffi'r afon? ('And you, Myrddin? Do you like the river?').

A command (the form that tells someone to do something) has a ti form and a chi form. Pennod 7 gave the ti forms; the chi forms, for more than one person or one person politely, are Dewch! ('Come!'), Ewch! ('Go!'), Edrychwch! ('Look!') and Arhoswch! ('Wait!'). Edrychwch adds -wch to edrych; arhoswch adds -wch to arhos-, with an h that aros lacks. Dere and dewch, cer and ewch are not built this way: learn them as pairs. This book uses only these four chi commands for now. Myrddin tells the children Arhoswch. Edrychwch ar y dŵr ('Wait. Look at the water'). But Mali, to Arth alone, says Edrych, Arth! ('Look, Arth!').
